1.note: Paired commas around nonrestrictive when-clause; B drops the opening comma, C the closing, D semicolon makes a fragment.

2.note: Past narrative needs approved/had been; C mixes past with present perfect, D reverses the sequence.

4.note: Waste is released on the tide; liberated/emancipated/saved misfit.

5.note: whom is object of knew; who would be subject case, whose/which ungrammatical.

6.note: Sentence foreshadows water-borne cholera the paragraph confirms; D's contradiction claim is false, B and C misdescribe the paragraph.

7.note: Concessive contrast (built for smell, yet unplanned effect); Nevertheless is slightly loose (However would be ideal) but no other choice competes.

8.note: from which ... drew; A doubles preposition with where, B wrong preposition, C redundant it.

9.note: Fixes the comma splice; C still a splice, D makes which ungrammatical.

10.note: Only D returns to the paragraph 3 detail (doubling pipe width); C recalls paragraph 2, B paragraph 4.

12.note: Removes redundant appositive; B awkward modifier, D still redundant.

13.note: Appositive after comma; semicolon and period create fragments, D a comma splice.

14.note: Complaint implies hogging; consulting is the normal use of reference books so it does not motivate a complaint; note only.

15.note: Times dismissal is an example of 'not everyone was charmed'; others illogical.

16.note: Semicolon joins two independent clauses; A and D are splices, C run-on.

17.note: Paragraph 4 is about Farrar's rules shaping the puzzle; others off-topic.

18.note: Parallel noun series (grids, words, clues); C clause breaks parallelism.

19.note: Plural subject rules (along with phrase does not change number) takes are; still implies present.

20.note: Example illustrates misleading without lying; others misstate content.

22.note: Comma sets off trailing participial phrase; D without comma reads 'slowly molting' as a unit, B/C create fragments. Note only.

23.note: Noun clause subject is singular; present tense matches 'still'.

24.note: Song sentence belongs right after the males singing, i.e. before the females sentence at [C].

25.note: Transitive present lay; laid would break present tense, lain is a participle.

26.note: Paragraph describes predator satiation as protection; attack/ambush/disguise misfit.

27.note: Contrasts the mass-emerging majority with a lone early/late insect.

28.note: Transitions from timing of emergence to cycle length (prime numbers).

29.note: Reflexive needed for subject antecedent; them would be ambiguous/ungrammatical, itself wrong number.

30.note: whereas gives the contrast and fixes the splice; because is illogical, semicolon + whereas leaves a fragment.

31.note: everyone's is the only correct possessive.

32.note: Colon introduces the list of the six; comma reads as seven items, semicolon needs independent clause.

33.note: Coaxing a cat down and the gentle weeks-long teaching imply patience; urgency/haste clash with coaxing. Note: urgency has slight pull as 'earnest' but does not fit the simile.

34.note: Sets up contrast with the narrator's terror; others misstate the paragraph.

35.reason: B is grammatical and a careful student can defend it as terror producing the conviction that water would rush in; the colon (explanation) is better because the conviction explains the terror, but the 'so' reading is sensible.
35.note: Colon introduces the explanation; B grammatical with arguably reversed causation.

36.note: Past perfect for an event prior to 'realized'.

37.note: strong is the idiomatic precise word; mighty/brawny/forceful are off-register.

38.note: Adverb slowly modifies swim; flat 'slow' is colloquial, not standard.

39.note: Contrast between still-weak swimming and walking into the lake.

40.note: Personal narrative, not a method; B false, C/D misjudge purpose.
